lead: Delta modulation (DM) is a one-bit differential coder. At every sampling instant it compares the input with a staircase built from past bits, and sends 1 if the input is above the staircase or 0 if it is below. The staircase moves by a fixed step Δ. Adaptive delta modulation (ADM) changes Δ with the signal slope. DM and ADM are used in low-cost speech links, voice storage and simple sensor telemetry where a low bit rate and simple hardware matter more than high fidelity.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 DPCM for prediction from past samples, Chapter 4.1 for sampling rate, and the slope of a sinusoid from Unit 1.

blocks.text: Delta modulation (DM) sends one bit for every sample. The transmitter keeps a staircase estimate x̂(t) of the input x(t). A comparator asks one question at each clock tick: is x(t) above or below x̂(t)? A 1 means above, a 0 means below. That single bit is transmitted. The same bit drives an integrator, which adds Δ for a 1 and subtracts Δ for a 0. So x̂(t) moves one step of Δ volts toward the input. Δ is the step size.

items: Sample the comparator output at f_s.
Send 1 if x(t) > x̂(t); otherwise send 0.
Move the staircase by +Δ for 1 and -Δ for 0.
Repeat at the next clock tick.

blocks.where: R_b is the DM bit rate in bits per second; f_s is the sampling rate in samples per second. DM sends one bit per sample.

blocks.text: At the receiver, an integrator repeats the same staircase from the received bits: +Δ for 1, -Δ for 0. A lowpass filter then smooths the staircase into an estimate of x(t). The receiver needs no code-word boundary or multi-level decoder, only the bit clock. The staircase is not the final audio; it is the running estimate. DM is the 1-bit limiting case of DPCM, covered in Chapter 4.5.

The staircase can change only by Δ at each sample, so its fastest possible slope is Δf_s volts per second. If |dx/dt| exceeds this, x̂(t) lags behind. The modulator then sends a long run of 1s or 0s, but the staircase still cannot catch the input. This is slope overload. It causes large errors on steep parts of the signal.

blocks.where: Δ is the step size in volts; f_s is the sampling rate in samples per second; f is the sinusoid frequency in hertz; A is its peak amplitude in volts. This is the no-slope-overload condition for x(t) = A sin(2πft).

blocks.text: For x(t)=A sin(2πft), dx/dt=2πfA cos(2πft). The largest magnitude is 2πfA. Slope overload is avoided when Δf_s is at least 2πfA.

A large Δ prevents overload but makes the staircase jump too far around a slowly varying input. The estimate then oscillates up and down near x(t), producing granular noise. A small Δ reduces this buzz but overloads on steep slopes. Fixed DM must choose one compromise between slope overload and granular noise. Granular noise is the DM quantization noise; it is not the same as slope overload.

sections.h3: Adaptive delta modulation and PCM comparison

blocks.text: ADM varies Δ with the signal. The receiver can deduce the same changes from the received bits, so no extra bits are sent. A common rule: after a run of equal bits (say three or four 1s, or three or four 0s), the staircase is being pushed one way, so multiply Δ by a factor above 1. When bits alternate, the staircase is hovering, so multiply Δ by a factor below 1. Keep Δ between Δ_min and Δ_max.

During steep slopes Δ grows, so ADM tracks without slope overload. During quiet parts Δ shrinks, so granular noise falls. This gives a more constant signal-to-noise ratio over a wide amplitude range than fixed DM. ADM still sends one bit per sample: R_b=f_s.

DM needs only a comparator, clock and integrator; PCM needs a multi-level quantizer and an n-bit encoder. PCM bit rate is f_s n, so 8 kHz speech with 8 bits is 64 kbit/s. DM at 64 kbit/s uses f_s = 64 kHz, one bit per sample. That high sampling helps slope tracking, but DM still has coarser quantization and a fixed-step trade-off. ADM improves dynamic range while keeping one bit per sample. For the same quality DM often needs a higher f_s than PCM, so its bandwidth is not automatically lower.
DM and ADM appear in low-cost voice recorders, simple telemetry and some speech codecs. DPCM in Chapter 4.5 generalizes the same prediction idea to n-bit differences.

figure.caption: The comparator, sampler and feedback integrator produce one bit per sample. The values are the worked example: x(t) is 1 kHz and 2 V, f_s = 32 kHz, Δ = 0.1 V.

spec.title: Delta modulator
spec.aria: The delta modulator compares the input with an integrator staircase, samples the comparator decision into one bit per sample, and feeds the bit back through the step-size integrator.

examples.question: A 1 kHz sinusoid of peak amplitude 2 V is encoded by delta modulation with step size Δ = 0.1 V and sampling rate f_s = 32 kHz. (a) Find the maximum slope of the sinusoid. (b) Find the maximum slope of the DM staircase. (c) Does slope overload occur? (d) Find the minimum f_s that avoids slope overload for this sinusoid with the same Δ.
steps: For x(t)=A sin(2πft), maximum slope = 2πfA. Here f=1000 Hz and A=2 V.
DM staircase maximum slope = Δf_s = 0.1×32,000 = 3,200 V/s.
examples.answer: Slope overload occurs; to avoid it f_s must be at least about 126 kHz (125,660 Hz using the rounded slope).
examples.check:
import math
f = 1000.0
A = 2.0
delta = 0.1
fs = 32000.0
max_slope = 2*math.pi*f*A
stair_slope = delta*fs
fs_min = max_slope/delta
print(int(round(max_slope)))
print(int(round(stair_slope)))
print(int(round(fs_min, -1)))

traps: DM bit rate is f_s, not f_s×n. One bit leaves every sample even though the staircase has many voltage levels.
A larger Δ reduces slope overload but increases granular noise. A larger step is not always better.
Slope overload depends on the maximum input derivative, not on peak amplitude alone. A small high-frequency sine can overload while a large slow sine does not.
The receiver integrator output is a staircase, not the final smooth signal. The lowpass filter after it produces the smooth estimate; it is not PCM reconstruction.
ADM adapts Δ from the received bit pattern. It does not send extra side bits, so its bit rate is still f_s.

quiz.q: State the bit rate of DM and define its step size.
quiz.a: R_b = f_s, one bit per sample. Δ is the voltage added to the staircase for a 1 and subtracted for a 0.

quiz.q: What does a transmitted 1 mean in DM?
quiz.a: The input x(t) was above the current staircase estimate, so the next staircase step goes up by Δ.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed step size force a trade-off in DM?
quiz.a: Large Δ avoids slope overload but increases granular noise. Small Δ reduces granular noise but causes slope overload on steep signals.

quiz.q: Define granular noise and say when it appears.
quiz.a: Granular noise is oscillation of the staircase around a slowly varying input when Δ is too large. It is the DM quantization noise.

quiz.q: A 1 V, 500 Hz sinusoid uses DM with Δ=0.05 V. Find the minimum f_s to avoid slope overload.
DM has f_s=16 kHz and Δ=0.2 V. Find the maximum staircase slope. Can it track a 2 V, 300 Hz sinusoid?
quiz.a: Δf_s = 0.2×16,000 = 3,200 V/s. Required slope = 2π×300×2 = 3,769.9 V/s. No: 3,769.9 > 3,200 V/s, so slope overload occurs.

quiz.q: Compare DM, ADM and PCM for a 64 kbit/s telephone speech link.
quiz.a: PCM at 8 kHz and 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s with good fidelity. DM or ADM at 64 kbit/s has f_s = 64 kHz and one bit per sample; hardware is simple, but fixed DM has a slope/granular trade-off and coarser quantization. ADM widens dynamic range. PCM is preferred for trunk speech; DM and ADM suit low-cost low-power links.

beyond: Not for the exam. Delta modulation is the simplest predictive coder, and its feedback staircase grows into delta-sigma (ΣΔ) modulation, the core of many audio and sensor ADCs. Continuously variable slope delta modulation (CVSD) is a practical cousin used in some Bluetooth voice links. Search for delta-sigma ADC, CVSD and adaptive quantization to see the descendants of this chapter.
